DDH.md:
## Who gets it
- Risk factors: **breech** (strongest), female, first-born, family history, oligohydramnios, tight swaddling with hips extended. **Left hip** in about 60%.
- Associated "packaging" conditions: torticollis, metatarsus adductus, congenital knee dislocation.

## Examination by age
- **Newborn:** **Barlow** (adduct + push posteriorly: dislocatable hip) and **Ortolani** (abduct + lift trochanter: dislocated hip reduces with a clunk).
- **After about 3 months:** these become negative. **Limited abduction** is the most reliable sign; **Galeazzi** (unilateral, knee lower); Klisic line.
- **Walking child:** Trendelenburg limp (unilateral), waddling gait and hyperlordosis (bilateral).

## Imaging
- **Ultrasound** until the femoral head ossifies (about 4-6 months). **Graf alpha angle** of 60 degrees or more is normal (type I). Type IIa (50-59 degrees, under 3 months) is physiological immaturity: re-scan. Lower angles and types III/IV need treatment. Femoral head coverage under 50% is abnormal.
- **Radiograph** after 4-6 months: Hilgenreiner and Perkin lines (head should lie in the inferomedial quadrant), broken **Shenton line**, raised **acetabular index**, delayed ossific nucleus. In older children and adults, a **centre-edge angle** under 20 degrees means dysplasia.

## Treatment by age
| Age | Treatment |
|---|---|
| 0-6 months | **Pavlik harness**: hips flexed 90-100 degrees, abduction not forced. Confirm reduction on ultrasound; stop if not reduced in 3-4 weeks |
| 6-18 months (or Pavlik failure) | **Closed reduction** under anaesthesia with arthrogram, adductor tenotomy, spica in the "human position" (about 100 degrees flexion, abduction within the Ramsey safe zone) |
| over 18 months | **Open reduction**, often with femoral shortening and pelvic osteotomy |
| beyond about 8 years unilateral (6 bilateral) | Usually leave a high dislocation unreduced |

- **Pavlik complications:** femoral nerve palsy (excess flexion), inferior dislocation, AVN (forced abduction), "Pavlik disease" (posterior wall erosion from persisting with a non-reduced hip).
- **Pelvic osteotomies:** **Salter** (redirection, 18 months-6 years, needs a concentric reduction); **Pemberton** (reshaping, capacious acetabulum, open triradiate cartilage); **Dega** (posterior deficiency, neuromuscular hips); after triradiate closure, **Ganz periacetabular osteotomy**.

## Blocks to reduction
- **Extra-articular:** iliopsoas (hourglass capsule), adductor longus.
- **Intra-articular:** pulvinar, hypertrophied ligamentum teres, transverse acetabular ligament, inverted labrum (limbus).
- The **medial (Ludloff) approach** in infants endangers the medial femoral circumflex artery.

> Exam pearl: **AVN of the femoral head** is the most important complication of treatment, not of the disease itself (Kalamchi-MacEwen classification).

Perthes and SCFE.md:
## Perthes disease (idiopathic AVN of the capital epiphysis)
- Age **4-8**, boys 4-5:1, bilateral in about 10-15% (asynchronous), delayed bone age. Symmetrical bilateral changes suggest **multiple epiphyseal dysplasia** or hypothyroidism instead.
- **Waldenstrom stages:** initial (dense epiphysis, **crescent sign**), fragmentation, reossification, healed.

| Classification | What it tells you |
|---|---|
| **Herring lateral pillar** (fragmentation stage) | A: pillar height normal. B: over 50% preserved. B/C border: about 50%, or a narrow or poorly ossified pillar. C: under 50%. Best predictor of outcome, together with age |
| Catterall I-IV | Extent of head involvement; "head at risk" signs: **Gage sign**, lateral calcification, lateral subluxation, horizontal physis, metaphyseal cysts |
| Salter-Thompson | Extent of the subchondral fracture: A under 50%, B over 50% |
| **Stulberg** (at maturity) | I-II spherical and congruent (good); III-IV aspherical congruence; **V aspherical incongruence** (worst) |

- **Prognosis:** **age at onset** is the most important factor (under 6 years does well), then lateral pillar class. Girls fare worse.
- **Treatment = containment.** Under 6 years: symptomatic care and range of motion. **Over 8 years with lateral pillar B or B/C:** surgical containment (proximal femoral varus osteotomy or Salter innominate osteotomy) gives better heads (Herring's multicentre study).
- **Hinge abduction:** valgus-extension osteotomy or shelf acetabuloplasty (salvage).

## Slipped capital femoral epiphysis (SCFE)
- Obese adolescents: boys 13-15, girls 11-13. Bilateral in 20-40%.
- Suspect an **endocrine cause** (hypothyroidism, growth hormone therapy, renal osteodystrophy) if under 10, over 16, or thin.
- The metaphysis moves anterior and externally rotated; the epiphysis stays posterior and medial in the acetabulum.
- **Signs:** obligatory external rotation on flexion (**Drehmann sign**); knee or thigh pain (obturator nerve referral). Never miss it in a child with knee pain.
- **Loder stability** (the key prognostic split): **stable** = can walk, AVN risk near 0; **unstable** = cannot walk even with crutches, AVN risk up to about 50%.
- **Imaging:** **Klein line** does not cross the epiphysis (Trethowan sign); Steel metaphyseal blanch sign. **Southwick slip angle** on the lateral view: mild under 30 degrees, moderate 30-50, severe over 50. The frog-leg lateral is the most sensitive view, but avoid it in an unstable slip.
- **Treatment:** **in situ fixation with one cannulated screw**, centred in the epiphysis, perpendicular to the physis, with no joint penetration. Do not reduce a stable slip.
- Prophylactic fixation of the other hip: endocrine cause, age under 10, open triradiate cartilage, poor follow-up.
- Severe or unstable slips: **modified Dunn** realignment through a surgical dislocation, in experienced hands.
- **Complications:** AVN (unstable slip, forceful reduction), **chondrolysis** (screw penetration), cam-type FAI.

clubfoot and foot deformities.md:
## Congenital talipes equinovarus (clubfoot)
- Deformity **CAVE**: **C**avus (plantarflexed first ray), forefoot **A**dductus, hindfoot **V**arus, **E**quinus.
- The talar neck is deviated medially and plantarward; the navicular is displaced medially. Twice as common in boys; half are bilateral.
- **Pirani score** (0-6: 3 midfoot + 3 hindfoot) and Dimeglio grade assess severity and track correction.

### Ponseti method
1. Correct the **cavus first** by **supinating the forefoot** (lift the first metatarsal) to line it up with the hindfoot.
2. **Abduct** the supinated foot around the **head of the talus** as fulcrum. Never press on the calcaneocuboid joint (**Kite's error**), and never pronate.
3. Weekly long-leg casts, usually 5-6.
4. **Percutaneous Achilles tenotomy** (needed in about 80-90%) once abduction of about 60-70 degrees is reached but ankle dorsiflexion stays under about 10-15 degrees; then 3 weeks in a cast.
5. **Foot abduction brace**: 70 degrees external rotation on the clubfoot side (about 40 on a normal side), 10-15 degrees dorsiflexion; 23 hours a day for 3 months, then nights and naps until 4-5 years.

- **Relapse** is mostly due to stopping the brace. Re-cast. Dynamic supination in a child over about 3 years: **tibialis anterior transfer to the lateral cuneiform**.
- **Complex (atypical) clubfoot:** short, fat foot, deep plantar crease, short hyperextended big toe. Use the modified Ponseti technique.

## Other foot deformities
- **Congenital vertical talus (rocker-bottom):** irreducible dorsal dislocation of the navicular on the talus. **Forced plantarflexion lateral view:** the talar axis still passes plantar to the first metatarsal and cuneiform (**oblique talus** reduces). Treat with **reverse Ponseti (Dobbs)** casting, then limited open pinning of the talonavicular joint and Achilles tenotomy. Associated with arthrogryposis, myelomeningocele and chromosomal syndromes.
- **Metatarsus adductus:** a kidney-shaped foot with a flexible heel; the **heel bisector** (Bleck) grades it. Most resolve; stretch or cast the rigid ones.
- **Tarsal coalition** (peroneal spastic flatfoot, recurrent ankle sprains):
  - **Calcaneonavicular:** age 8-12, **"anteater" sign** on the oblique view. Excise and interpose EDB or fat.
  - **Talocalcaneal (middle facet):** age 12-16, **C-sign** on the lateral view; CT is the test of choice. Resect (with fat interposition) if the coalition is under about 50% of the subtalar joint surface and there is no arthritis; otherwise fuse.
- **Flexible flatfoot** is physiological if the arch appears on tiptoe and the hindfoot swings into varus. Treat only if painful.
- **Cavovarus foot in a child:** look for a neurological cause (Charcot-Marie-Tooth, spinal dysraphism). MRI of the spine if unilateral or progressive.

paediatric fractures.md:
## Physeal injuries
- Physeal fractures pass mostly through the **zone of hypertrophy** (provisional calcification).
- **Salter-Harris:** I (through physis), **II (most common**, metaphyseal Thurston-Holland fragment), III (epiphysis, intra-articular), IV (across metaphysis and epiphysis), V (crush, worst growth prognosis, often recognised late). Rang added type VI (perichondral ring injury, peripheral bar).
- Growth arrest: bars under 50% of the physis in a child with over 2 years' growth left are excised with interposition (fat or cement); larger bars need epiphysiodesis or correction.

## Elbow
- **Supracondylar humerus:** commonest elbow fracture (age 5-7); **extension type** in over 95%.
  - **Gartland:** I undisplaced; II hinged on an intact posterior cortex; III completely displaced; IV multidirectionally unstable.
  - Nerves: **AIN is the commonest** injured nerve in extension type. Posterolateral displacement of the distal fragment endangers the **median nerve and brachial artery**; posteromedial displacement endangers the **radial nerve**. The flexion type injures the **ulnar nerve**.
  - Treatment: closed reduction with **2-3 divergent lateral pins** (no ulnar nerve risk). A medial pin adds stability but risks iatrogenic ulnar injury.
  - **Pink, pulseless hand** after reduction: observe closely. **White, pulseless hand:** explore the brachial artery.
  - **Cubitus varus** from malunion is the commonest late complication; Baumann angle helps judge the reduction.
- **Lateral condyle:** over 2 mm displacement needs ORIF. Non-union leads to cubitus valgus and **tardy ulnar nerve palsy**.
- **Medial epicondyle:** often with elbow dislocation. **Incarceration in the joint** is an absolute indication for surgery.
- **Monteggia:** in children, **Bado I** (anterior radial head dislocation) is commonest. Always check the **radiocapitellar line** in every forearm fracture.

## Femur and hip
| Age | Femoral shaft treatment |
|---|---|
| 0-6 months | Pavlik harness or splint |
| 6 months-5 years | Immediate hip spica |
| 5-11 years | **Flexible (titanium elastic) nails** if length-stable and under about 45-50 kg |
| over 11 years or heavy | **Lateral-entry rigid nail** (avoid a piriformis entry: AVN risk) or submuscular plate |

- **Delbet hip fractures:** I transepiphyseal (highest AVN risk), II transcervical (most common), III cervicotrochanteric, IV intertrochanteric. Treat as emergencies: urgent reduction, fixation, capsulotomy.

## Ankle (transitional fractures)
- The distal tibial physis closes **central, then medial, then lateral**.
- **Juvenile Tillaux:** SH III avulsion of the anterolateral epiphysis by the AITFL.
- **Triplane:** SH IV in three planes.
- CT the joint; **over 2 mm articular displacement needs reduction and fixation**.

## Non-accidental injury
- High specificity: **classic metaphyseal lesions** (corner or bucket-handle), **posterior rib fractures**, scapula, spinous process and sternum fractures, multiple fractures of different ages.
- A **femoral fracture in a non-walking child** needs a skeletal survey. A toddler's fracture (spiral, distal tibia) is usually accidental.

cerebral palsy and neuromuscular.md:
## Cerebral palsy
- A **non-progressive brain lesion** with **progressive musculoskeletal deformity**. Spastic diplegia is typical of prematurity (periventricular leukomalacia).
- **GMFCS I-V** describes function and predicts hip displacement (risk rises steeply from level III to V).
- **Hip surveillance:** regular AP pelvis radiographs, **Reimers migration percentage**.
  - Over 30-40% in a young child: soft-tissue release (adductor longus, gracilis, iliopsoas).
  - Over 40-50%, or older: **varus derotation osteotomy with pelvic (Dega) osteotomy**.
  - Spastic hips sublux **posterosuperiorly**.
- **Tone management:** **botulinum toxin** for dynamic spasticity in young children. **Selective dorsal rhizotomy** for spastic diplegia, GMFCS II-III, age about 4-8.
- **Gait patterns:**
  - True equinus and jump gait.
  - **Crouch gait**, often after over-lengthening the Achilles.
  - **Stiff-knee gait** from an overactive rectus femoris: **distal rectus transfer**.
  - Surgery for several levels is done in one sitting (**single-event multilevel surgery**, about age 6-10).
- **Silfverskiold test:** equinus that corrects with knee flexion means **isolated gastrocnemius** contracture (Strayer or Vulpius recession). If it does not correct, both gastrocnemius and soleus are tight (tendo-Achilles lengthening).
- **Scoliosis** in non-ambulant children: long C-shaped curves with pelvic obliquity. Fuse to the pelvis.

## Muscular dystrophies
- **Duchenne:** X-linked, absent **dystrophin**; boys 3-5 with **Gowers sign**, calf pseudohypertrophy, **CK hugely raised**; non-ambulant by about 12.
  - Scoliosis develops once wheelchair-bound. Fuse early, when the curve is about 20-30 degrees and **FVC is still adequate (over about 30-35%)**.
  - Corticosteroids delay loss of walking and reduce scoliosis. Watch for cardiomyopathy.
- **Becker:** abnormal (reduced) dystrophin, milder and later.

## Other neuromuscular disorders
- **Spinal muscular atrophy:** SMN1 deletion, anterior horn cell loss, symmetric proximal weakness, absent reflexes. Hip subluxation is usually left alone. Nusinersen and gene therapy have changed the outlook.
- **Myelomeningocele:** the **motor level** decides walking (functional quadriceps, L3-L4, is the key). Hip dislocation at L3-L4 is usually not reduced. Watch for latex allergy. **Tethered cord** (rapid curve progression, new deformity, spasticity) needs urgent MRI.
- **Charcot-Marie-Tooth (HMSN I):** PMP22 duplication; **cavovarus foot**. A weak tibialis anterior is overpowered by peroneus longus (plantarflexed first ray); a weak peroneus brevis is overpowered by tibialis posterior. The **Coleman block test** shows whether the hindfoot varus is flexible (forefoot-driven). Usually treat the forefoot first.
- **Friedreich ataxia:** GAA repeat in frataxin; ataxia, scoliosis, cavus feet, **cardiomyopathy** (main cause of death).
- **Arthrogryposis:** multiple congenital contractures with normal sensation and intelligence. Rigid clubfeet and dislocated hips are common.

skeletal dysplasias.md:
## Remember the genes
| Condition | Defect | Key features |
|---|---|---|
| **Achondroplasia** | **FGFR3** gain-of-function, AD (about 80% new mutations, older fathers) | Rhizomelic shortening, frontal bossing, **trident hand**, champagne-glass pelvis, **interpedicular distance narrows caudally**, **foramen magnum stenosis** (infant apnoea, sudden death), thoracolumbar kyphosis, adult **spinal stenosis**, genu varum. Vosoritide (CNP analogue) increases growth |
| Hypochondroplasia / thanatophoric | FGFR3 | Milder / lethal |
| **Pseudoachondroplasia** | **COMP** | Normal face and normal length at birth, short limbs from about 2 years, joint laxity, **odontoid hypoplasia**, early OA |
| **Multiple epiphyseal dysplasia** | COMP or type IX collagen | **Bilateral symmetrical** epiphyseal irregularity (mimics Perthes), early OA |
| **SED congenita** | **COL2A1** (type II collagen) | Short trunk, **atlantoaxial instability**, **myopia / retinal detachment**, coxa vara |
| Kniest | COL2A1 | Dumbbell femora, joint stiffness, retinal detachment |
| **Diastrophic dysplasia** | **SLC26A2** (sulfate transporter) | **Hitchhiker thumb**, cauliflower ears, rigid clubfeet, cervical kyphosis |
| **Cleidocranial dysplasia** | **RUNX2** | Absent or hypoplastic clavicles, open fontanelles, supernumerary teeth, coxa vara |
| Metaphyseal chondrodysplasia | Schmid: COL10A1; Jansen: PTH/PTHrP receptor (hypercalcaemia); McKusick: RMRP | Schmid looks like rickets with normal biochemistry |
| **Osteogenesis imperfecta** | **COL1A1 / COL1A2** (type I collagen) | Sillence I mild, blue sclerae; II lethal; **III most severe survivable**, progressive deformity; IV normal sclerae |
| **Mucopolysaccharidoses** | Lysosomal enzymes | **Morquio (IV):** keratan sulfate, normal intelligence, **odontoid hypoplasia (C1-C2 instability)**. **Hurler (I):** intellectual disability |
| **Osteopetrosis** | Osteoclast failure (carbonic anhydrase II, CLCN7, TCIRG1) | Bone-in-bone, Erlenmeyer flask, **rugger-jersey spine**, marrow failure in the infantile form (stem-cell transplant) |

## Principles
- **Proportionate** short stature is usually endocrine or nutritional; **disproportionate** suggests a dysplasia. Rhizomelic (proximal) vs mesomelic vs acromelic shortening.
- **Screen the upper cervical spine** (flexion-extension films or MRI) before anaesthesia in Morquio, SED, pseudoachondroplasia, Down syndrome and Larsen syndrome.
- **Osteogenesis imperfecta:** cyclic **bisphosphonates** reduce fractures. Long-bone deformity: multiple osteotomies with **telescopic rods** (Sofield-Millar osteotomies, Fassier-Duval rod). Watch for basilar invagination and hearing loss.
- **NF1:** anterolateral tibial bowing leads to **congenital pseudarthrosis of the tibia**. **Dystrophic scoliosis** (short, sharp curves, rib penciling, vertebral scalloping) progresses and needs early fusion.
- **Ollier** (multiple enchondromas) and **Maffucci** (with haemangiomas, higher malignancy risk) are sporadic. **Hereditary multiple exostoses** (EXT1/EXT2, AD) cause forearm deformity (ulnar shortening).

bone and joint infection in children.md:
## Why the metaphysis?
- Slow flow in the metaphyseal sinusoidal veins, gaps in the capillary endothelium and few phagocytes make it the commonest site for **acute haematogenous osteomyelitis**.
- Where the metaphysis is **intra-articular** (**proximal femur, proximal humerus, radial neck, distal lateral tibia**), osteomyelitis can burst into the joint and cause septic arthritis.
- In infants under about 18 months, **transphyseal vessels** let infection cross into the epiphysis and joint.

## Organisms
| Setting | Usual organism |
|---|---|
| All ages | **Staphylococcus aureus** (including MRSA; PVL-positive strains cause severe multifocal disease and DVT) |
| **6 months-4 years** | **Kingella kingae**: mild signs, near-normal markers, needs PCR or blood-culture bottles |
| Neonates | Group B streptococcus, Gram-negative bacilli, S. aureus |
| **Sickle cell disease** | **Salmonella** (characteristically), S. aureus |
| Nail through a sneaker | **Pseudomonas** |
| Unvaccinated child | Haemophilus influenzae type b |

## Septic hip vs transient synovitis
- **Kocher criteria:** **non-weight-bearing, fever over 38.5 C, ESR over 40 mm/h, WBC over 12,000**. Probability of septic arthritis with 0, 1, 2, 3 and 4 criteria is about 0.2%, 3%, 40%, 93% and 99.6%.
- **CRP over 2 mg/dL** (Caird) is a strong added predictor.
- Ultrasound confirms the effusion. Aspiration gives the diagnosis.
- **Septic arthritis is a surgical emergency:** arthrotomy and washout (anterior approach for the hip), then antibiotics.

## Imaging and treatment
- Plain films show bone changes only after **10-14 days**. **MRI** is the investigation of choice for osteomyelitis (marrow oedema, subperiosteal abscess).
- **Antibiotics:** a short IV course, then **early switch to oral** once the child is improving and CRP is falling. Typical totals are about **3 weeks for septic arthritis** and **3-6 weeks for osteomyelitis**.
- **Drain** a subperiosteal or intraosseous abscess, and operate when there is no response in 48-72 hours.
- **Complications:** physeal arrest, AVN of the femoral head, **pathological fracture**, chronic osteomyelitis, DVT (MRSA). Neonatal septic hip can destroy the head (**Tom Smith arthritis**).

## Chronic and subacute forms
- **Brodie abscess:** subacute osteomyelitis; a well-defined metaphyseal lucency with a sclerotic rim that can cross the physis. Differentials are osteoid osteoma and Langerhans cell histiocytosis.
- **Chronic osteomyelitis:** **sequestrum** (dead bone), **involucrum** (new periosteal bone), **cloaca** (opening). Treat by sequestrectomy after the involucrum is strong enough, plus antibiotics.
- **Chronic recurrent multifocal osteomyelitis (CRMO):** sterile, multifocal, clavicle and metaphyses. Treated with NSAIDs, not prolonged antibiotics.
- **Tuberculosis:** consider it in an Indian child with a monoarthritis or dactylitis (spina ventosa). Spinal TB is covered in Spine notes.
